title: Contextual Causal Bayesian Optimization
one_liner: Find the best intervention by using both context clues and knowledge of what causes what.
lead: Imagine you are tuning a factory to maximize output. You know some context (temperature, material quality) and you know which machines affect each other. Before this paper, people used either context OR causal knowledge, but not both together. This paper unifies them: a single method that looks at the context, follows the causal chains, and picks interventions that work best.

paras: Before this paper, Bayesian optimization split into two camps. One camp used contextual information: you observe some side facts (material type, time of day) and use them to predict which actions will work well. The other camp built causal models: you draw a graph showing which knobs really affect which outputs, and use that structure. A naive approach tries them one at a time and gets stuck.

The first camp's approach (contextual optimization) ignores the causal graph entirely, so it wastes time tweaking variables that do not actually move the needle. The second camp's approach (causal optimization) ignores the context, so it fails when the best intervention depends on what you already know about the situation. In high-dimensional settings where many variables exist, both methods stumble.

callout.html: Use context clues and causal structure together to find the best intervention.

steps.text: Look at the situation (temperature, material, time).
Which variables, in this situation, would actually influence the target?
Ignore variables that do not appear in any causal path for this context.
Use Bayesian optimization only over the relevant variables and their policy.
After each trial, refine the model of what context tells us and what causes work.

paras: The paper jointly optimizes two things: the intervention policy (which knob to turn and by how much) and the set of variables that the policy is allowed to touch. In simpler methods, the policy always depends on the same fixed set of variables. This paper says: the best policy variables change depending on the context and causal structure.

hidden.name: Causal relevance weight
paras: The hidden quantity is how much each variable matters for reaching the target in this specific context. Not all variables are always relevant. A temperature knob might matter if you are working with a chemical compound, but not if you are working with a metal. The paper measures this by tracing causal paths from each variable through the graph, conditioned on what the context is.

In traditional causal optimization, every variable in the causal graph gets considered equally. This paper instead computes a weight for each variable based on: how many causal paths lead from it to the target, and how strong those paths are in this context. Variables with higher weights get tried first.

heat.caption: Darker means more impact on the target in this context. Highlighted variables are on causal paths to the outcome.

reads.html: Some variables are on the causal path from your action to the result; others are not. The paper figures out which ones matter in this situation.
The method computes importance via causal path analysis, conditioning on context, and ranks variables accordingly for the intervention policy.

mechanism.h2: Why finding the right policy variables reduces confusion
paras: Bayesian optimization works by building a guess about which settings give good rewards (a model that says where the peaks are) and exploring smartly. The hard part is the search space: if you have many variables, the space of possible settings grows enormous and you get sparse information. You need many, many trials to explore it.

The paper's move is to shrink the search space. Instead of saying the policy can touch any variable, it says: only variables on causal paths to your target, given this context, go into the policy. The rest are locked. This cuts the dimensionality down dramatically. A smaller search space needs far fewer trials to explore, because there is less ground to cover.

This works because the locked variables do not actually help anyway (they do not cause changes in the target, given causality and context). By excluding them, you are not losing anything real, but you are gaining speed: the algorithm converges faster because it has fewer misleading dead ends to chase.

stages.s: Trace causal paths from each variable
Keep only variables on paths to target
Build Bayesian model over shrunk space

math.words: Total cost equals sample waste plus regret penalty, where the policy is designed to touch only variables on causal paths in this context.
math.equation: L(pi, S) = sum_t (y_t - y*) + lambda * |S|, where pi is the policy, S is the variable set, y_t is the reward at trial t, y* is the best possible reward, and lambda trades off policy complexity against sample efficiency.
symbols: the policy (which knob to turn, how much, given context)
the set of variables the policy is allowed to use
the reward measured in trial t
the best reward the context allows
the cost of adding variables; higher lambda shrinks S
how many variables are in the set

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose you have 10 variables, but only 3 are on causal paths in this context.
If the policy tries all 10, it wastes effort and needs 100 trials to explore all settings.
If you lock 7 and optimize over 3, you need only 30 trials to find the best setting (because fewer dimensions = faster exploration).
So: trials(all 10) = 100. trials(causal 3) = 30. Sample_waste saved = 70 trials.
The policy shrinkage (using only variables on S) directly shrinks regret, because you explore a smaller, more focused space.

math.note: Locking irrelevant variables shrinks the search space, so you need fewer trials to find the best setting.

charts.title: Naive method (all variables)
charts.note: Wastes effort on variables not on causal paths; slow convergence in high dimensions.

charts.title: This paper (smart variable set)
charts.note: Focuses only on causal variables in context; reaches high quality with fewer trials.

items.html: If the graph is misspecified (you think A causes B but it does not), the method locks out real levers and gets stuck. The method only works if the causal structure is correct.
If the context has no real effect on which variables matter, using context adds noise. The method assumes context shifts the causal relevance; if it does not, you lose.

items.b: Rare causal path in this context.
items.html: A variable might be off the causal path for 99 percent of context values but needed for the remaining 1 percent. If your context falls in that 1 percent, the method will not use that variable and will find a worse result.
When the causal graph is accurate and context genuinely shifts which variables are relevant, the method shrinks the search space without losing any real options, and convergence is fast.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic factory setting with a known causal graph (e.g., temperature and viscosity affect yield; pressure affects temperature; material type shifts which paths matter). Sample a context value (material type). Run three optimizations: one using all variables, one using only the context-relevant variables, and one using neither context nor causality. Measure the number of trials needed to reach a target quality (e.g., 90 percent of the peak yield).
demo.metric_eq: sample_efficiency = (trials_all_vars - trials_causal_smart) / trials_all_vars, as a percentage saved
demo.closing: The demo must show that when context and causality align, using both saves samples in high dimensions, because the method excludes irrelevant variables and thereby shrinks the space to explore. The savings grow larger as you add more irrelevant variables, because more get locked out.
